stem: When counseling a solid-organ transplant candidate about posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD) risk, which factor is described as the most important?

options.text: Transplantation of an Epstein-Barr virus–seropositive donor organ into an Epstein-Barr virus–seronegative recipient
A history of seasonal allergies without Epstein-Barr virus mismatch
Donor age younger than 18 years in every case regardless of viral serostatus

explanation.rationale_correct: The most important risk factor for PTLD is transplantation of an Epstein-Barr virus–seropositive donor organ into an Epstein-Barr virus–seronegative recipient.

rationale_incorrect.B: ABO blood type is not described as the primary PTLD risk factor.
rationale_incorrect.C: Epstein-Barr virus donor-recipient mismatch is the key risk described.
rationale_incorrect.D: Young donor age alone is not identified as the most important PTLD risk factor.

stem: An Epstein-Barr virus–seronegative adult receives a solid-organ transplant from an Epstein-Barr virus–seropositive donor. What primary-infection risk should the coordinator include in pretransplant counseling?

options.text: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection occurs in approximately 70% to 80% of seronegative recipients
Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection never occurs after transplantation
Primary infection occurs in fewer than 5% of seronegative recipients
Epstein-Barr virus infection is limited to donors and cannot affect recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infections occur in approximately 70% to 80% of Epstein-Barr virus–seronegative recipients, typically during the first six months post-transplant.

rationale_incorrect.B: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection is common in seronegative recipients after transplant.
rationale_incorrect.C: The referenced incidence is much higher than 5%.
rationale_incorrect.D: Recipients can acquire primary Epstein-Barr virus infection from the community, allograft, or blood products.

stem: During pretransplant infectious-disease teaching, which clinical presentation should the coordinator associate with posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD)?

options.text: Fever, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, or symptoms resembling infectious mononucleosis
Isolated acute graft tenderness without any systemic symptoms in every case
PTLD always presents with obvious skin rash and never with fever
PTLD cannot involve the gastrointestinal tract or lungs

explanation.rationale_correct: PTLD may present with symptoms resembling infectious mononucleosis, fever, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, weight loss, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or pulmonary lesions.

rationale_incorrect.B: PTLD may be asymptomatic or present with systemic symptoms rather than isolated graft tenderness alone.
rationale_incorrect.C: Fever and mononucleosis-like symptoms are described presentations.
rationale_incorrect.D: PTLD may involve the gastrointestinal tract, lung, kidney, or other sites.

stem: When explaining posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD) management options during evaluation, which initial treatment principle aligns with standard references?

options.text: Immediate intensification of all immunosuppression without evaluation
No change in immunosuppression because PTLD is always benign
Routine daily bone marrow biopsy as the only treatment option

explanation.rationale_correct: Treatment options for PTLD include reduction or withdrawal of immunosuppression, with additional therapies such as mTOR inhibitors, rituximab-based regimens, or radiotherapy depending on disease severity.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppression is reduced or withdrawn rather than intensified as initial PTLD management.
rationale_incorrect.C: PTLD represents a spectrum from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphoma requiring treatment.
rationale_incorrect.D: Immunosuppression modification is a primary treatment approach rather than biopsy alone.
